summary: Steve Ruiz presents tldraw's journey bringing AI agents onto an infinite canvas. tldraw is simultaneously a free online whiteboard, a London startup, and a hackable React-based canvas SDK used by Replit's agent canvas, Luma AI's canvas, and Stitches (annotate mode). Ruiz builds cool things with the SDK to prove its capabilities, increasingly involving AI. He starts with Make Real (2023), letting non-technical users draw on a canvas, send it to a vision model, and receive a working HTML prototype—an early 'break containment' moment before vibe coding was coined. Next came one-shot AI collaboration where the model used structured text outputs to produce canvas shapes (draw a cat, complete a graph), solving tricky problems around vision models and structured data: less vision training data than text and conflicting conventions (Y-axis direction, left/right ambiguity). Then came an agentic loop (likened to Cursor in 2025) that produces, reviews, and iterates, used in design apps like Lovelace and Magic Path and in education as a tutor. But this still felt like handing a keyboard to AI rather than collaborating. The breakthrough was fairies—agent avatars living on the canvas, making agent state, actions, and relative positions visible. Multiple fairies work simultaneously, see each other's work, or collaborate with one elected as leader who scouts, creates a to-do list, and delegates. This required solving shared state, leader-follower patterns, and preventing overlap among essentially blind agents. The fairies demo is at fairies.tldraw.com. Ruiz then describes the next frontier: giving agents more canvas access. Sandboxing won't work because they need the DOM, the browser, and screenshots. Instead, over the holidays he built an Electron wrapper around tldraw, opened a local HTTP endpoint that treats posted content as JavaScript and runs it—an approach he acknowledges is dangerous but acceptable for an offline, file-based desktop app. Agents can script-inject into the editor, make drawn UIs interactive, and even modify local desktop files. Anecdotes include fairies building an ebook reader and a teammate having Claude remove podcasts from Spotify by editing minified bundle code. Live demos were finicky. Ruiz connects this to local-first and file-over-app philosophies: previously idealistic ideas now become the only practical way to expose an app to agents locally. He calls these 'sharp tools' and references Open Claude as doing this well, ending with an invitation to try the fairies and follow tldraw on X.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: tldraw is an online whiteboard, a London startup, and a React-based canvas SDK used by Replit, Luma AI, and Stitches (annotate mode).
Make Real (2023) let non-technical users turn canvas drawings into working HTML prototypes before vibe coding was coined.
Vision models struggle with structured canvas output due to less training data than text and conflicting conventions (Y-axis direction, left/right ambiguity).
tldraw evolved from one-shot generation to agentic loops, but that still felt like handing a keyboard to AI rather than true collaboration.
'Fairies' are agent avatars on the canvas making state, actions, and spatial relationships visible across multiple concurrent agents.
When fairies collaborate, one is elected leader who scouts, creates a to-do list, and delegates, requiring shared state and overlap management.
Sandboxing agents won't work because tldraw needs the DOM, browser rendering, and screenshots; instead Ruiz built an Electron desktop app with a local HTTP endpoint that executes posted JavaScript.
Agents happily script-inject into tldraw and modify local desktop files (e.g., removing Spotify podcasts by editing minified code), making this a powerful but dangerous approach.
Local-first and file-over-app philosophies, previously curiosities, become practically necessary to maximize agent agency by exposing apps locally to agents like Claude.
Ruiz frames these as 'sharp tools' to hand to users at their own risk, referencing Open Claude as a precedent.

sections.title: Introduction to tldraw
sections.summary: Steve Ruiz introduces tldraw as a free online whiteboard, a London startup, and a React-based canvas SDK used by Replit, Luma AI, and Stitches. His job includes building cool things with the SDK to prove its capabilities, increasingly involving AI.

sections.title: Make Real demo
sections.summary: Ruiz demos Make Real (2023), one of the first apps to break AI containment, letting non-technical users draw on canvas, send to a vision model, and get a working HTML prototype. Users could annotate on top to iteratively refine. He jokes about leaked API keys and a demo that didn't fully cooperate.

sections.title: One-shot AI collaboration on canvas
sections.summary: Ruiz describes AI producing canvas shapes via text structured outputs (draw a cat, make the cat blow out a candle), solving hard problems around vision models and structured data: less training data than text and conflicting conventions like Y-axis direction and left/right ambiguity.

sections.title: Agentic loop and its limits
sections.summary: tldraw built an agentic loop (like Cursor in 2025) that produces, reviews, and iterates. Used in design apps (Lovelace, Magic Path) and education (tutor, D&D character sheet). But it still felt like handing a keyboard to AI rather than collaborating.

sections.title: Fairies: agents on the canvas
sections.summary: Ruiz introduces fairies—agent avatars on the canvas making state, actions, and spatial relationships visible. Multiple fairies work simultaneously, see each other's work, or collaborate with one elected as leader who scouts, creates a to-do list, and delegates. Orchestrating shared state and preventing overlap among blind agents was key.

sections.title: Safety and next steps
sections.summary: Ruiz demos fairies generating app wireframes and notes the next step is giving agents more canvas access, which runs into safety barriers around what is safe for users with a hackable runtime API.

sections.title: Desktop app, script injection, and local-first agents
sections.summary: Ruiz explains sandboxing won't work because they need the DOM, browser, and screenshots. Instead he built an Electron wrapper around tldraw exposing a local HTTP endpoint that runs posted JavaScript—an dangerous but acceptable approach for an offline file-based desktop app. Agents script-inject into the editor, make drawn UIs interactive, and even modify local files. Anecdotes include fairies building an ebook reader and a teammate having Claude remove Spotify podcasts by editing minified code. Live demos were finicky. Ruiz connects this to local-first and file-over-app philosophies, now practically motivated by needing to expose apps to agents locally. He calls these 'sharp tools,' references Open Claude, and invites the audience to try the fairies and follow tldraw on X.

demonstrations: Make Real: drawing sent to vision model produces working HTML prototype, then annotated to refine colors
One-shot AI: draw a cat, make the cat blow out a candle, draw a mouse—multiple prompts on different canvas areas
Agentic loop: draw a diagram of the life cycle of a butterfly with produce-review-iterate cycle
Fairies: multiple agents on canvas, one elected leader scouts and delegates to others to draw animals
Fairies wireframing: summoning fairies to make wireframes for an app from a description
Desktop app: fairies building an ebook reader via script injection into Electron-wrapped tldraw
Interactive UI: drawing a UI with leg-length and t-shirt-color controls and asking AI to make it interactive
Spotify anecdote: Claude removing podcasts from Spotify by editing minified bundle code
limitations: Vision models have much less training data than text

Agents are essentially blind while working, risking overlap
Sandboxing agents won't work because the DOM, browser, and screenshots are needed
Script-injection endpoint is dangerous and not recommended for web apps

Agents will modify local desktop files without hesitation, creating real risk
